A hopeful rebirth for the old-school MMO formula.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

World of Warcraft: Forever has, much as the original World of Warcraft did back in 2004, completely consumed my life. I write about games for a living, mind, so the attention vortex it has wrought upon me is primarily professional obligation, rather than just irresponsibility.

What is it?: A reimagining of 2004's World of Warcraft, with new balancing, lighting, dungeons, and items.Expect to pay: A monthly subscription of $14.99/£10.99. Optional race and early-game zone behind a £25.99/$30 paywall.Developer: Blizzard EntertainmentPublisher: Blizzard EntertainmentReviewed on: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060, AMD Ryzen 7 5800 8-Core Processor, 16GB RAM, Force MP600 SSDMultiplayer?: YesLink: Official site

But at the time of writing, it has been 443 hours since Forever's launch. I have spent 147 of those hours asleep (less, but let's just pretend I've been getting a solid eight), leaving around 296 hours of my waking mind. 230 of them have been spent playing World of Warcraft.

That's a deeply concerning amount of time if I wasn't getting a salary to review it—it has been part of my 9-5. I've also often been keeping the game open while I, you know, feed and bathe myself and do chores. So we're probably just in the realm of 'moderately worrying' rather than 'cause for a wellness check'.

Don't worry, I intend to take a break soon: But during those 230 hours, I have hit level 60, entered 31 dungeons, completed 941 quests, levelled engineering, mining, and first aid to 300, and apparently /waved at other players 50 times. Which are rookie numbers that I need to get up.

But I've also found myself taking in the scenery, laughing at my poor luck at bottles, whining about the drop rates of basilisk brains, splitting mining nodes with party members, mercilessly grinding ogres into paste for my first mount, and talking to more strangers while questing than I have in years of playing more modern, streamlined MMOs.

I'm not pointing this out to simply cast aside the role of nostalgia in my enjoyment, but I do think nostalgia can only carry an attention span so far. It certainly doesn't keep 230 hours of medically inadvisable gameplay afloat on its own. There's something else going on here; something special that's been unearthed.

All of the things that made an old-school MMO like the original WoW so deeply enthralling back in 2004 are not simply dated, to be cast aside as an inferior form of videogame.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

The crappy drop rates, the fighting over tags, the running everywhere (there is so much running everywhere) while not always justified, is part of an experience that's stronger for its inconveniences. The friction burn you get from jutting up against a game that's occasionally just hostile to you. All of that connects you to the world, and the people in it, in a very real way.

First, I want to talk about what Forever itself has actually brought to the table. After all, much of what I've talked about already has been reverence paid to a series of design decisions that were made over 20 years ago.

In the here and now, though, Forever has around 1,000 new quests (the original WoW is estimated to've had somewhere in the mid-2,000s, so that's approximately 30-50% more Warcraft), nine new dungeons, and two new major levelling zones in Mount Hyjal and The Riverglades.

To encourage and support levelling alts, Blizzard's added a new mechanic in the Legacy tree—a genuinely cool feature that encourages you to level alts (or do endgame achievements and raids) to unlock perks, like making levelling slightly easier by giving you a small heal when you kill an enemy in the open world, or by giving you more resources when you gather things.

Then there's the retooled class and item balance, the latter of which is my one, very mild point of disappointment: There's an increasing amount of trinkets and weapons I've kept around for specific use cases, sure, but at least while levelling, the fantasy of equipping an anti-worgen sword to do some worgen-killing quests (as so often quoted in Blizzard's promotional material) hasn't quite panned out. That's not to say it's gone by the wayside completely, though.

I've seen a two-handed axe that lets you get mining nodes, a knife that lets you skin humanoids, gloves that increase your mining skill, boots that let you walk under water, and so on. It's just not a core part of the levelling experience.

It does also improve somewhat when you get into the later levels. For instance, I now have a two-handed questing sword green that I'll keep in my bags basically forever because it lets me spin around like a propeller to slow my fall speed: And I'm a Warrior, so that's a hugely useful traversal tool for someone without any way to slow fall.

Professions have also had a total facelift, and for the first time, I'm actually levelling crafting and gathering skills on my characters because of it.

Not only do crafting ones like blacksmithing actually give you really good gear as you level up (rather than just a couple of big capstone items) but all professions can now turn in writs and crates, buying new recipes via the latter and unlocking them with a rep grind via the former.

The new zones are both excellent—the Riverglades is pretty, but not out of place, whereas Hyjal is a satisfying (and very efficient) climb up a mythological mountain ruined by war, with some legitimately cool questlines to it. In both, questing is enough of a breeze that it does feel almost too easy, with Hyjal smoothing over the typically arduous 58-60 grind completely. But they're not any more efficient than, say, The Burning Crusade's better zones, which is a level of kayfabe-breaking I can get behind.

But until you hit that point, Forever's newness is downright subtle. A chain here, a few fetch quests there. Just enough to make questing in every zone worth it, just enough to even out the occasional, clunky speedbumps.

With Riverglades being level 38, and Mount Hyjal not mattering until the final stretch, Forever partially buries the lede, and you'd be forgiven for thinking it a touch unambitious. But with Blizzard's commitment to add new Riverglade-style zones and questlines to the game in the years to come, it's going to keep morphing into something new with the passing years, and what's there—when you get to it—is plainly impressive.

Such as Forever's new dungeons. I've done seven out of the new nine crawls, and while they're a little more mechanically dense than the vanilla predecessors (bosses sometimes have like, two moves) I've been fascinated by just how well that old-school design has been emulated.

With the exception of Alcaz Island, these things are sprawling, time-consuming romps. And, while controversial, the changes to dungeon XP (putting the majority of it in their quests while lowering the amount you get from mobs) has made completing them an adventure.

I recently knocked out Sunken Temple's questline, but the world-trotting, multiple quest-chain journey to get all my pre-requisites had me doing another unrelated dungeon a second time, fighting my way to the top of a troll fortress in the Hinterlands, helping out a drunk dwarf, and speaking to the spirit of a fallen Horde warrior to get his hipflask.

So when it was time to finally darken the door of the Sunken Temple and get it all done, I felt accomplished. Like I'd not just rocked up to a portal to get some fat loots, but that I'd actually—like an adventurer might—spent considerable time researching, preparing, and bracing myself for the place.

Didn't stop us forgetting that the Shade of Eranikus summons all the currently-alive dragon adds to him and getting absolutely mauled, but hey-ho.

More to the point, my XP reward for that journey felt considerably far more potent than if I'd simply hopped in there to rinse it 5 times. And I might have skipped it if the XP reward wasn't mostly dispensed via questing. I won't say dungeon XP isn't an issue for some players, but for me, the exercise works.

There hasn't just been an RTX-on style filter slapped over Azeroth, this is all bespoke."

And while you're running around the world, forced to jog ignobly between major locations, Forever's new lighting system and draw distance shines through. The reason these lighting changes aren't in retail yet is because, primarily, they're hand-crafted.

Durotar has these darling oversaturated blue shadows, Felwood bathes everything in a sickly green, Duskwood's mist hangs thick in the air, and the lightning that crackles over the Blasted Lands actually casts electric blue light across the stones of Nethergarde Keep.

But there are subtle changes, too. You can see Nordrassil, the world tree at the top of Mount Hyjal, from Durotar—as well as other zones on the continent. Dun Morogh and Winterspring have uniquely hostile snowstorm blizzards that cut out visibility entirely, similar to Tanaris' sandstorms.

There hasn't just been an RTX-on style filter slapped over Azeroth, this is all bespoke, and it's made all of my journeys that much more atmospheric. I've had to stop just to take in the godrays pushing through the canopy of Ashenvale, or the burning sunset descending on the seas of Stormwind Harbor.

More importantly, these effects really pull out the strengths of that old-school mode of design. Both the 2004 version of World of Warcraft and Forever understand that in order for a world to feel massive, it needs to be difficult to traverse sometimes. In order for it to be social, there needs to be a level of unfairness that being social will overcome.

I thoroughly enjoyed World of Warcraft: Midnight, the latest expansion in modern World of Warcraft, when I reviewed it for launch. I thought the questlines, which I can remember the glossy cinematics and major storybeats of, were engaging enough. And I still think its new revamped Silvermoon is gorgeous, and a complete flex from the studio's art team.

I could not, however, tell you a single thing about my questing experience that wasn't dictated to me by the game. Yes, I liked certain story beats or character conversations, but the actual experience of hitting stuff? It's a blur. I flew somewhere, I pushed my buttons, I interacted with something. I flew somewhere else, and you know what I did there? I pushed more buttons.

In contrast, I've been playing Forever for almost three weeks, and I've already made memories. On a jog to an annoying Scarlet Monastery dungeon questline that sent me to Desolace, I met up with two dwarven brothers (or husbands? They had the same second name) who were making the journey. We joined up with more people to kill a bunch of high-level skeletons, and barely got through an overpull by the skin of our teeth.

In Stranglethorn Vale, a kindly shadow priest six levels higher than me partied up to kill some pirates, then pointed out that there was a good questline that could be done by scavenging beach bottles. They got theirs on their first try. I, for some reason, had to pick up 26 of the damn things.

On another journey, I decided to try and grab my fire-hardened mail armor for a warrior questline, which sent my alliance character all the way into The Barrens, to Razorfen Kraul. This is not a great dungeon to do if you're an alliance character, so the pickings were slim. Which meant that I not only tanked the whole thing as Fury, but that the folks I was with were chill enough to do a quick road-trip to Feralas with me to get another dungeon quest.

The point being, I only had these memorable experiences and spoke to these people because I was being, and I know this is a bad word for a lot of MMO players, inefficient. Absolute bastard questlines made me do something far out of the way. And every single time I've played along, I wound up having a lovely time meeting similarly stubborn folks and making new friends.

A lot of these inconveniences, carried over from vanilla and left alone in Forever, are there to push you and people you meet organically, out in the world, into close quarters and camaraderie. To do "kill X" quests, you need to intentionally party up with that random night elf warrior, rather than just pass them by. To get certain questlines accomplished at the level they're given, you need to ask for help in general chat.

Some chains will send you to some random city, forcing you to learn the most efficient boat route to get there—or to simply leave that quest in your log until you next happen to pop your head into Darnassus. The travel time makes the world feel big. The encouraged cooperation makes it feel alive and social. And all that friction produces friendships—these quests suck to do on your own but are so often a breeze to do together. Or, at the very least, they're more entertaining with company.

This is why it doesn't just feel like nostalgia to me. It's the rub of the whole thing. I am not enjoying these quests because, at some time in the past, I had a nice innocent memory surrounding them that I'm reliving. It's actually all about what's happening in the present: Grouping up with people, striking up conversations, sharing in misery as it takes a full 45 minutes to fill our bags with pirate hats.

I'm honestly just marvelling about the fact that, in 2026, that this sort of design still works. It works tremendously well. Blizzard's new campfire mechanic, which I like a lot, is just a cherry-on-top-nudge towards striking up the conversations I was already having anyway.

So many times, my purposefully chill vibes have been met with genuine kindness: People stay on to help you finish quests they've already completed, they show you new questlines. Sometimes it's a tit-for-tat. A shaman helped me out with my level 50 warrior quest in exchange for me helping him kill an elite somewhere, which hey, fair dos.

This all culminated in an incident where I joined in for a random kill quest in my mid-40s. A priest, around their mid-40s as well, commented that man, a lotta folks had their mounts already! Myself included. I'd spent a few hours mining over 200 Iron Ores and killing cave ogres, like a maniac.

I asked how far off they were. They said they had 80 gold out of 90. I threw 15 gold at them before I realised what I was doing.

This isn't to humblebrag, mind. My grinding had produced a surplus of cash that I wasn't really spending: But it was like I'd been suddenly possessed by the spirit of Christmases past, future, and present. I gave a complete stranger a significant amount of money with the complete understanding I'd never talk to them again. Because I felt like being nice, because so many people had been nice to me.

I do understand the yearning for flight paths, for lower respec costs, for shared mob tagging, and for quests that don't require your character to walk the circumference of the earth. And if none of that's to your taste, then hey, fine—but more than anything, Forever's proven to me that those flying mount doomers back in The Burning Crusade might've been onto something.

I still enjoy 'theme park' MMOs, but Forever is such a deeply exciting prospect to me. It's a second chance for this older, slower, more social form of videogame to have a renaissance. Before booting up Forever on November 4, I couldn't tell you the last time I had an adventure (an organic one, not one delivered to me through a storyline) in an MMORPG. Two weeks later, and I've had several, and I keep logging on and embarking on these long, arduous quest chains because I'm excited to have more.

Forever is such rare air. A major MMO studio has been given the blessing to revamp a 20+ year old version of a game and add to it. And while it's already added a considerable amount, Forever feels like proof that, given enough exposure in the spotlight, people could actually like a new MMO with its design sensibilities.

And as a fan of lots of different kinds of MMOs—be they slow-paced adventures like Forever or on-rails dungeon-rinsing theme parks like Final Fantasy 14—I want this genre to have the kind of actual diversity it deserves. More MMOs than World of Warcraft should get to take this sort of risk. More MMOs should be able to take it slow.

Until that new game comes, however, I'll happily play Forever, and I cannot wait to roll up an alt to start doing it all over again.

A hopeful rebirth for the old-school MMO formula.

Harvey's history with games started when he first begged his parents for a World of Warcraft subscription aged 12, though he's since been cursed with Final Fantasy 14-brain and a huge crush on G'raha Tia. He made his start as a freelancer, writing for websites like Techradar, The Escapist, Dicebreaker, The Gamer, Into the Spine—and of course, PC Gamer. He'll sink his teeth into anything that looks interesting, though he has a soft spot for RPGs, soulslikes, roguelikes, deckbuilders, MMOs, and weird indie titles. He also plays a shelf load of TTRPGs in his offline time. Don't ask him what his favourite system is, he has too many.

#3824. GTA 6 breaks the all-time livestream viewer record hours before it's available to play for most of the world

Hours before it's even playable in most of the world, Grand Theft Auto 6 has already broken the record for the most viewers across livestreaming platforms like Twitch.

According to streaming data and analytics website Streams Charts, GTA 6 had amassed 6.38m live viewers across Twitch, YouTube, and Kick at 12:30 UTC today. At that time, the game had been officially available for a few hours in New Zealand, and elsewhere by using a region-switch trick.

The previous record for most live viewers was set by Valorant, Riot Game's popular tactical shooter, during its closed beta in xx. That game brought in 1.74m live viewers, but it's worth noting there was a promotion offering players a chance to access the beta if they watched a stream. Despite having no such incentive, GTA 6 has more than tripled Valorant's record.

Twitch is the largest platform for GTA 6 streams according to Streams Charts, and already the game is the 6th biggest category in Twitch history. It's also expected the figure will increase as GTA 6 launches officially in more regions of the world.

If you'd like to find out when exactly Grand Theft Auto 6 releases for you, check out Eurogamer's GTA 6 launch time guide for an accurate list by country. You can also read the Everything We Know about Grand Theft Auto 6 guide for a full breakdown on all the details ahead of its launch in your region.

#3823. Fish with a sniper rifle takes aim at Tim Sweeney's hopes and dreams, as genAI-free meme game tops Epic Games' vibe-coding megajam

Epic Games are, as you're probably aware, going big on genAI at the moment. To the extent that, last month, the Tim Sweeney-helmed company announced the Epic AI MegaJam. Build a playable game in Unreal Engine or Unreal Editor for Fortnite with help from as many AI agents or tools as you like was the pitch.

So, naturally, sorting the submissions by 'Popular' turns up a game about a fish with a sniper rifle whose creator says they deliberately made it without using any generative AI.

The game's called LSD:FIH and sees a cigarette-smoking bit of shoe-wearing marine life go full MLG and start pulling off trickshots on blobs. If you struggled to parse that, you'll probably struggle even more with developer PolyCube's description of it as being a "computer game about a fih aura-farming". "No AI was used to make this game," is the other line in their description, which is far easier to parse.

"I made a game for the Epic's 'vibe-coding gamejam' megajam without using any AI in four days," they expanded on not Bluesky. "Sorta ran out of time so gameplay didn't turn out how I wanted, but hey it's still pretty aura."

Other submissions the megajam included a game called THIS GAME IS AI SLOP and one dubbed Goon Patrol - Director's Cut. If you're wondering how a game without genAI use could be allowed to stand among the slop masterpieces, it's because Epic ended up having to make clearer not long after the jam was announced that submissions didn't have to make use of genAI as a hard rule, leaving it up to the developer how much or little was worked in.

Still, I imagine noted genAI advocate Tim Sweeney's not best pleased that a game deliberately swimming against the slop tide shows up at the top if you hit up the Popular filter. Then again, he's been very busy posting important things about the situation with Jensen Huang and Nvidia lately, so maybe he hasn't noticed.

Yes, the last post I've linked there is the Sweens giggling at an AI image of him, Huang, Johan Andersson, and John Carmack as the heads carved into Mount Rushmore that he himself asked Grok to generate. As you do.

Leonida deserves to be explored with friends.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I honestly can't recall the last time I took such delight in existing within a virtual world as the way I have with Grand Theft Auto 6's Leonida. Rockstar has delivered on its promise of both breadth and depth—the map is huge, but utterly stuffed with detail. Large, open highways shrink into single lanes surrounded by construction that force me to slam the brakes. Sidewalks sparse with pedestrians eventually lead to densely packed retail areas, restaurants, and clubs.

Pockets of culture erupt all over: the sheer redneckery of Port Gellhorn, the Latin culture that permeates Little Cuba, and the affluent snootiness of Capri that has cops flinging microaggressions in every direction. You don't need to undertake any missions in these areas to understand the people that live here—Rockstar has nailed so much of the environmental storytelling and the conversations between NPCs you'll stumble on as you roam.

It's a world that, when I first ventured into it, I had no interest in exploring in a multiplayer setting. I spent an ungodly amount of time in GTA 5's Online mode when it first released. I was there on the ground for its incredibly shaky launch (I made a character and then got stuck in that birdseye view loading screen for hours, incredible stuff) and continued to sink time into it over the years, particularly during Covid.

And I like it well enough, but its novelty has waned over the last decade. Its core experience is inherently different from what singleplayer brings, and I had yearned to return to a world less about blowing other players up with flying motorbikes and more about, well, blowing non-players up with regular motorbikes.

But after 60 hours roaming around Leonida and witnessing what it has to offer? I now want nothing more than for Rockstar to spin this map into the next generation of Online. Even outside of missions and driving around, there are so many little things that I would kill to do with pals.

Grab a pack of brewskis from the convenience store, hop in a boat, and go fishing. Throw on our best all-American attire and get down and dirty in some mud racing. Seek out other players meticulously planning a jewellery store hold-up, only to swoop in and steal the goods for ourselves. Hit up the gym for a little workout before nipping to a nearby restaurant for a bite to eat. Leonida is a place that is so rife with things to do, and I can imagine doing almost all of them with some buddies by my side.

It's also the perfect opportunity for Rockstar to introduce things that are sorely missing for me right now. A lack of safehouses makes sense with GTA 6's offline story, but I yearn to buy highrise apartments and suburban houses. Maybe even buy a business or two, for a little side cash. There's also the matter of that gigantic casino and the go-kart track that are currently inaccessible but the latter of which is donning a large "COMING SOON" sign. It feels like I'm being taunted. Surely you wouldn't put these things in the game with no intention of opening them at some point… right?

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

And even as someone who was never interested in nor dabbled with GTA Online's flourishing roleplaying scene, I've encountered so many instances where I've thought roleplaying in Leonida actually be pretty darn neat. I could become a RydeMe driver, or a Snapmatic influencer, or a backwater recluse who lives off the land. And when the game comes to PC? The potential for bending the world to account for even more professions becomes all the greater.

Rockstar hasn't actually said a damn thing about GTA 6 Online right now, but it feels inevitable. Leonida is the biggest playground the developer has given players to date, and unleashing players across its sprawling map is Online's natural evolution. And, y'know, considering how much money GTAO has made over the last 13 years, I'm almost certain that Rockstar won't leave that kind of opportunity on the table.

Mollie spent her early childhood deeply invested in games like Killer Instinct, Toontown and Audition Online, which continue to form the pillars of her personality today. She joined PC Gamer in 2020 as a news writer and now lends her expertise to write a wealth of features, guides and reviews with a dash of chaos. She can often be found causing mischief in Final Fantasy 14, using those experiences to write neat things about her favourite MMO. When she's not staring at her bunny girl she can be found sweating out rhythm games, pretending to be good at fighting games or spending far too much money at her local arcade.

#3820. GTA 6 is so big, it managed to break Reddit - and it isn't even actually out yet

Grand Theft Auto 6 isn't even out yet, and it's already causing some technical issues over at the game's official Reddit page.

In a post verified by r/GTA6 moderators and pinned to the page, user and moderator PapaXah wrote "GTA 6 broke Reddit", and explained that "many things" were currently busted at the time of the post. Looking through Reddit, many flairs (little labels attached to posts) aren't loading properly and appear as a string of code rather than proper images. PapaXah also replied to one user suggesting they make real flairs based on these busted flairs, writing: "Reddit's so broken I couldn't even do it. We actually have a bunch of new flairs that I can't even upload."

Another moderator, TekS, also acknowledged that some user's posts may not be viewable as a result of ongoing strain on Reddit during GTA 6's release. They commented: "If you can't post/comment or see your user flair, well, know that it's perfectly normal."

Ahead of the game's full launch across the world, the Grand Theft Auto 6 has already broken viewership records across streaming platforms like Twitch and YouTube. Interesting details about the game are also trickling out, including the fact that different refrigerators have their own unique sounds. Video games, ladies and gentlemen.

With Grand Theft Auto 6 releasing today, our review has been released to the wild with it. It is overwhelmingly positive, with Chris Tapsell dubbing GTA 6 as "the most believable and unbelievable video game world ever made" and rated it a full five stars.

#3819. Ubisoft lay off 166 more staff, this time at their Montreal and Quebec City studios, while mumbling about "current production priorities and business needs"

"Our production needs are changing," publishers claim

Ubisoft have laid off 166 developers, with this latest round of cuts at the Assassin's Creed and Far Cry publishers taking place at two of their studios in Eastern Canada. Both studios affected, Ubisoft Montreal and Ubisoft Quebec, had a hand in last year's Assassin's Creed Shadows, with Montreal especially being a major and long-tenured development hub for the company.

Both IGN and GamesIndustry.biz report that the cuts, which amount to just under 4% studios' total combined headcount, affected staff working on recently cancelled or significantly changed projects.

"Ubisoft is reducing its workforce by 166 positions across its Montréal and Québec City operations," Ubisoft said in a statement handed to both sites. "As our portfolio evolves, our production needs are changing, requiring us to adjust the size of some teams to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs.

"We deeply value the contributions of these teams and recognise the impact this may have on our colleagues. We are committed to supporting them through this process with care and respect. Those affected are being provided with severance, extended health care benefits, career transition services and other resources."

Ubisoft Montreal are currently working on Assassin’s Creed Hexe, reportedly a witchy tale set during the time of the Holy Roman Empire, which switched creative directors earlier this ear and is one of the games Ubi are keen to get out of the door. What Quebec have been up to since Shadows shipped is less clear. They're a much smaller than Montreal and were founded in 2005.

Ubisoft have been carrying out mass cuts across their studios worldwide all the way through this year. Ubisoft Singapore and Trials developers Redlynx. Ubisoft Winnipeg, Belgrade, and Barcelona. Long-time Tom Clancy studio Red Storm. Ubisoft's Paris HQ. Three German studios including Anno devs Ubisoft Mainz. All have been subjected to some form of cuts or closure.

Meanwhile. changes to remote working policies have also contributed to strikes at Ubisoft studios in France and Italy.

Solidarity to all of the Ubisoft workers who've been affected by these layoffs in Montreal and Quebec.

Here's how you can get NOS boost for your cars in GTA 6 and how to use it

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Using GTA 6 NOS to give your car a boost can be helpful in street races and just for getting around, but the game doesn't make it very clear how it's used with some easy-to-miss prompts. In short, it's a bit like having a sprint for your car, so it's pretty simple to use, but I've explained how it all works in GTA 6 just below.

To use nitrous in GTA 6, you must hold L3/LS while fully pressing R2/RT. If you press in the left stick while at anything other than full throttle, you'll just honk your horn instead.

Obviously, you must also be driving a GTA 6 car that has Nitrous Boost installed. Any Mod Shop can install this component for you for $5,000, and it's found under the Performance tab, then the Boost section – depending on the car, it can also provide small boosts to its speed and acceleration stats. Otherwise, cars with NOS already installed are incredibly rare but there's a Declasse Yosemite 1500 called the Nutbusta that comes with nitrous that you can steal for Moses in Chapter 2, so you might want to keep that rather than sell it.

You can tell a car has NOS installed because it'll have a blue ring icon next to the engine health and fuel gauges. You can only use your NOS boost in short bursts as the blue ring indicating how much nitrous you have will rapidly empty when using it. Conveniently it refills on its own unlike regular gas as you need to refuel your car in GTA 6.

But bear in mind that, from my experience using the nitrous boost in GTA 6, the extra speed isn't that spectacular, with the camera field-of-view and zoom out making it feel faster than it actually is. It's certainly not unhelpful for street races, but don't expect it to surge you into first place.

And if you're wondering what car is in all the images in this article, it's the GTA 6 Paul Walker car – incredibly, it doesn't come with NOS as standard, but I had to fit it as soon as possible to make it just like the car in The Fast and the Furious.

#3816. All 34 of the infamously fired Rockstar staff appear in GTA 6 game credits, though some aren't listed as "former employees", curiously

UPDATE: The final few names have been confirmed.

UPDATE 19TH NOVEMBER: All of the 34 fired Rockstar employees appear in the credits for GTA 6. We were able to confirm the final few names' existence there after Rockstar posted the full credits online - in searchable form. Before this, the process of cross-checking was intensely laborious: it required watching a scrolling list of names for an hour-and-a-half to see if they appeared.

Also, we couldn't identify six names in the "former employees" section of the credits before because they don't appear there, we now know. These names appear listed under the departments the people worked for, as if they still worked at Rockstar. Why this is, we don't know - perhaps it's something to do with being involved in the employment tribunal or not. We're asking Rockstar for clarification.

ORIGINAL STORY 18TH NOVEMBER: Eurogamer can confirm that at least 28 of the 34 employees fired by Rockstar roughly a year ago - in an action that directly led to the employment tribunal Rockstar is currently facing in Scotland - are named in the credits of Grand Theft Auto 6.

A number of those fired employees are seeking compensation for unfair dismissal amid allegations of "union busting", in an employment tribunal that comes to an end today. The delayed climax of the case couldn't be more fateful, aligned as it is with tomorrow's release of GTA 6, and the outcome will be historic either way.

Rockstar recently revealed that more than 4,711 people worked at the company making GTA 6, employed across 12 offices around the world - a staff-count that has more than doubled since Red Dead Redemption 2. It's a game that's wowed critics - Eurogamer awarded GTA 6 five stars in our review this afternoon - and which observers expect to generate $2bn in revenue in its opening weekend alone.

But perhaps Christian Donlan put it best when digesting the opulence on display in the Netflix 'extended look' GTA 6 trailer. "To spend all this money making something so beautifully rich and detailed, to pay billions for this game and sweat every little animation, to float it out to us on Netflix, amongst genuine discussion around whether Netflix can handle it? That's commitment," he wrote. "And if you're willing to do that, and willing to do that to tell an underdog story, you should let your workers who made everything form a union."

#3815. Ignore that other game about crime that's out and burgle some ugly farmhouses in Keepsake County, a "midwestern stealth game" with a 2000s Cartoon Network vibe

Is there something going on today? A lot of talk about committing crimes and the like, I just can't quite put my finger on why… Ah well, couldn't be important or interesting. What is interesting, however, is Keepsake County, a "midwestern stealth game" that has launched on this inauspicious day about stealing stuff from "hideous farmhouses in the middle of nowhere."

With the sarcastic intro out the way, I will address the elephant in the room: Vovly's Adventure: Reslimed is out today too. Fine, fine, yes I know GTA 6 is the game everyone's talking about, but Forward Instinct, the devs behind Keepsake County, seem well aware of that in their launch day post for the game: "Folks, thanks for your incredible patience. Keepsake County is finally OUT! And yes, it is deeply ironic that it wound up being today, of all days, that we got the green light to finally release, but here we are."

Keepsake Country was supposed to release earlier this month, but seemingly got caught up in the backlog Valve are faced with that's undoubtedly been caused by genAI games. In any case, the burgle-em-up does look quite delightful. I'm not sure if I can quite put my finger on exactly why I get this feeling, but it calls to mind a more complex version of the kind of game you'd find on Cartoon Network's website back in the day (which is a high point of praise, I'd like to be clear).

Each house in Keepsake Country is procedurally generated, meaning you never quite know what to expect when you enter. There's lockpicking, resident tie upping, and of course stealing to be done, but it doesn't just stop at the house. Parking your car, for instance, is an important thing to consider; do you want it hidden so you're less likely to be discovered, or right at the front door so you can make a speedy escape? Not to mention you have to deal with the fuzz showing up at some point if you aren't quick enough!

Gear and the like can be improved between runs, meaning you can lockpick faster or delay the cops, it all seems quite systemically thoughtful. Very much some immersive sim vibes from this one, just on a much smaller scale. And most certainly worth considering picking up on a release day like today! If you're interested in doing so, you can pick it up on Steam right here.

The world wants me to write more about Grand Theft Auto 6 and I bravely answer "No". Last week, I obtained 50% of the endings available in Queen's Domain, the best videogame to release in the year 2026. The next 50% require, well, a lot of nook-scouring and cranny-uncovering—many more hours of gameplay which I am preserving for myself as a Christmas holiday treat.

And when I do, I suspect I might make a little (just a little) use of this rad Queen's Domain map by a creator called Leny15. Barely a week ago I wrote that "I suspect a cross-section of [Queen's Domain's] goliath, entwined map would make for a killer bit of wall art". Well, I was right. Here it is and it looks rad as hell.

No, really. Even if you're not a Queen's Domain player—or maybe especially if you're not—take a look at this thing. It's one thing to wander these maps as a player, it's another to get a totally flexible birdseye view of how dense, twisty and interconnected they are. I will never stop being blown away by how knotty and elaborate this game is; I love it.

I will also never believe I have actually explored all of it. I'll be honest, gang, I really feel like I've plumbed the depths of this game, but this map has entries for areas I ain't even heard of, and even those areas that I have heard of seem to contain secret sub-areas I've barely touched.

My favourite feature of this thing has got to be the ability to upload your save to it, at which point it will give you a completion percentage and tick off the collectibles and secrets you've already attained (reminder that you can download your Steam cloud saves right in your browser). I was heartened to read that I have, it seems, done in about 70% of this game already. I was even more heartened to learn that the remaining 30% seems even stranger, more complicated, and more baffling than all the rest. I can't wait to check it out.

#3813. PSA: Some GTA 6 Ultimate Edition content is only available for the first chapter, and you'll have to put in hard graft to unlock more

GTA 6's Ultimate Edition has proven enormously popular, despite its hefty $100 price tag. So much so that Strauss Zelnick, boss of Rockstar parent company Take-Two, recently confirmed it's the edition most people are buying - and that's despite a lack of specific information about how its unlockable content works. With GTA 6 just hours away from release, however - and out now in certain parts of the work - details are beginning to emerge, and the answer is perhaps a little surprising.

As previously confirmed, the $100/£90 Ultimate Edition provides access to exclusive vehicles, weapons, shops, and more, with the full list as follows:

Rockstar also previously revealed that "Ultimate Edition bonuses become available to Jason and Lucia across their story, with new items uncovered behind each chapter". The specifics of how - and when - all this stuff unlocks, though, remained unclear. So if you've opted for the Ultimate Edition, you might be wondering where your stuff is when you finally fire up the game. As reported by IGN, which has full unlock details, it turns out virtually all of GTA 6's Ultimate Edition content, as per details in the in-game shop, requires progressing through the main story - in some cases dozens and dozens of hours into the story - before it'll become available.

Ultimate Edition-exclusive shops, for instance, unlock during Chapter 1, and many of the other additions become available by the end of Chapter 2. That doesn't sound too difficult, but as Eurogamer's Chris Tapsell notes, reaching that point could take upward of 25 hours. As for some of the late-game unlocks, such as the Shitzu Squalo and the Vice City Style outfits and tattoos (available in Chapter 4) and Chapter 5's 95 Grotti Cheetah, you could be looking at closing in on 60 hours of playtime before they unlock.

"It'll vary depending how hard people focus on the main story," Chris explains, "but if you were mostly focused on the main story plus the optional character-based missions in largely chronological order, that's about how long it'd take."

It's also worth noting - perhaps surprisingly - that some Ultimate Edition content is only a temporary unlock, usable only during specific chapters. Jason's Dinka Enduro motorcycle and Crest Kayak, for instance, can only be accessed and enjoyed during Chapter 1. That's also true for his retro Vapid Ganado, available from the Coastal Auto Care mod shop in Key Lento. So basically, you'll want to make the most of these while you can!

All this might be a little disappointing for players who were expecting to be showered with Ultimate Edition spoils from the off (and that they'd be permanent unlocks), but the good news is 60 hours in GTA 6 is far from a chore. As Chris explained in his five star GTA 6 review, Rockstar's latest is an "irreducible mix of silliness, intimacy, grand ideas and rock 'n' roll action" that "pushes back the horizon of video games once again".

PlayStation creator Ken Kutaragi isn't so sure we'll have consoles at home in the future – in fact, he believes we might not need them at all one day.

Speaking with The Game Business in a new interview, Kutaragi first explains that things are just… well, way too pricey. "Currently the machines are super expensive," as he admits. "It's not a healthy situation. You spend huge money on [them, because] graphics boards are super expensive right now." Then there are all the RAM shortages and other hardware issues (many spurred by the rise in AI) that are contributing to these high prices.

It doesn't help that, as Kutaragi notes, Sony and Microsoft have moved toward more PC-like architecture for PlayStation and Xbox consoles. Sure, it makes developing games that can launch on all systems a bit easier, but, again, the hardware costs a lot. "It worked, but right now PC is super expensive – it's the price of a car, it's not healthy." The former PlayStation executive touches on AI, too, which isn't all too surprising.

After all, Kutaragi himself now serves as the president and CEO of Cyber AI Entertainment, having previously predicted that, uh, AI daydreams could replace video games someday. As per the founding PlayStation father, the controversial tech (AI, that is) is "evolving [into a] much more elegant thing," and we'll see its impact in gaming. "The age may be coming where we don't need any consoles. It's a [real] danger."

The evolution of AI might lead to "some lightweight platform," he ponders – but it won't be akin to the PS5 or Xbox Series X|S. "It will not be a console, it will not be a smartphone." Kutaragi does clarify, though, "This is not the official comment from Sony Interactive Entertainment!" And, again, he feels pretty optimistic about AI and how it might change entertainment – even if that means the death of consoles.

"Everything can be calculatable. The AI is elaborating, but it's at an intermediate stage. Maybe in the future, everything [will] be calculatable. Everything. If those things happen, what entertainment could we and our children create for the future? Those things will not take several decades. Maybe it will be coming very, very soon. Be prepared for that." I'm not sure I want to be, honestly – but I suppose anything is possible.

The shift away from physical media – just see Sony's highly controversial decision to end all physical disc production – doesn't help, I'm sure.

#3810. Space station horror-FPS Derelikt is a lively retro throwback to Alien: Resurrection, though it's better at shooting than scaring

I'm a reasonable man. I don't expect every PS1-styled, cosmic horror, nakedly Alien: Resurrection-homaging retro FPS to suffocate me under a blanket of misery. Some of the lighter moments in Derelikt, which released last week, even land: I was grinning my cheeks off as I gorged on the Eldtrich knowledge sealed within an alien obelisk, while repeatedly hanging up on the aghast scientist who kept videocalling me to stop.

Still, Derelikt is fortunate that it's a good shooter, as it often gets muddled on whether it wants to be a horror game as well. It certainly threatens the spooks, trapping you in an oppressively dingy asteroid rig in the orbit of Saturn - the scariest of the ringed gas giants! - and warping most of the other staff into vaguely echinodemic monsterpeople. Also, opening the inventory reveals it to be made of rectangles, a classic symptom of a video game character about to get mangled in the nerves and face.

But nah, shotgun go boom boom. It turns out Derelikt's derelict dwellers are both perfectly susceptible to mundane lead, and sparing users of ambush tactics at most; several even stand around with their backs turned, as if waiting for you to surprise them with a lethal pipe swing. And, even on Medium difficulty, the opening spell of fight-or-run scarcity quickly gives way to an abundance of ammo and health pickups that can easily fill the pocket grid to bursting. I don't claim to have been playing perfectly, but I'm about halfway through and the only way I see myself running low on bullets is if I start using them to punch the complete works of Thomas Campion into a wall.

It's indecisive tonally, as well. The dialogue, and there are a fair few survivors to chat with, seems interested in emulating the gravitas-starved, "Woah man" style of New Millennium action game scripts. Which I can sort of see the logic behind, given the visuals and sound design also, and arguably much more painstakingly, mimic that era. But the downside remains that it ends up with a gravitas-starved, "Woah man" style, just with an extra dash of sideways-winking awareness. Again, it only sometimes works, and it's never scary or eerie. But then there are also more earnest attempts to spin uneasiness, with pages of deranged scribbles left behind by the dwindling crew, and at least a couple of genre-classic wall daubings, which tend to leave me wishing developers Visuwyg had just picked a lane.

Again, though, underneath all the smartarsing is a quality little shooter. The retro presentation does little to soften the heavy, industrial kick of its gunfire, and although many of the meatier freaks are more absorbent than they look, their pained thrashing really helps sell the impact of every individual shot. I also don't really mind the lack of Dead Spacey surprise attacks, as the station's narrow confines tend to force you into tenser, close-range encounters in an organic way anyhow.

More impressive still is how Derelikt manages to fabricate a cold, apprehensive atmosphere befitting its fallen space base, in direct defiance of its own quasi-comedic script. This is mainly thanks to the clanging, low-lit station itself, which teases you with just enough flashes of comfort – a stretch of marble floor here, a messy rec room there – to make your quick return to its steel guts feel all the more unpleasant. Some credit must also go to the puzzling, the cardkey hunts and code searches of which initially had me fearful of the more obstinate, opaque, classic horror style preferred by fellow backwards-looker Silver Pines. Instead, it's more like a compacted Deus Ex, hinting at the need to peek at people's computers and scour the environments for the needed codes. Which makes for generally smoother progress, yes, but also gets you more involved and present inside Derelikt's infested walls.

Midway-through impressions, then: it's a little silly, and perhaps a little confused, but Derelikt finds its focus whenever something needs making dead. I shall continue blasting xenos and burning my eyes out with magic rocks until – no, madam, please hold – further notice.

#3809. Even the PS5 Pro is "not powerful enough" to run GTA 6 at 60FPS or 40FPS, Rockstar says

Don't expect GTA 6 to get an update supporting higher framerate modes, at least, not on current-generation consoles. Rockstar has explained that even the most powerful console of the bunch, the PS5 Pro, isn't powerful enough to run the lavish game at 40FPS or 60FPS.

Last week, some players weren't too happy with the news that GTA 6 is targeting 30FPS on all platforms it's currently launching on - PS5 Pro, PS5, Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S. Like countless other big productions this generation, the hope was that Rockstar Games would offer both quality and performance modes for its lush open-world monster.

Rockstar's now seemingly confirmed that its crime epic won't run at 60FPS or 40FPS anytime soon, simply because it can't on the currently available hardware.

"While the PS5 Pro's central processor is slightly better than the PS5 base console, it is not powerful enough to run the game's complex simulation at higher frame rates," the studio's technology production director, Marc Chambers, said in a statement to Kotaku. There you have it, then - even the beefiest console around can't handle Leonida at higher framerates.

Chambers did note some of the souped up console's other technical improvements, however: "Our base presentation makes use of ray-traced reflections and global illumination. On the PS5 Pro, this is enhanced with the addition of ray-traced shadows, as well as overall added clarity through the use of PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR). The PS5 Pro features an upgraded graphics processor and upscaling technology that we leverage to increase the game's visual fidelity."

The tech gurus over at Digital Foundry gave some more insight into how GTA 6 runs on current-gen machines, calling it a "technical tour de force," though one that can still dip below 30FPS on PS5 and Xbox Series X during busier chase scenes and explosive shootouts. It's perhaps unsurprising, then, that higher framerates are off the table for now.

A 30FPS launch is by no means a departure for Rockstar Games, either. GTA 5 also ran at an unsteady 30FPS when it first dropped onto the Xbox 360 and PS3, with 60FPS support only coming alongside the game's PC port more than a year later. I'm not too fussed about the game's 30FPS target, personally. I'd much rather have a game that consistently hits 30FPS than one that continuously chugs trying to reach 60FPS, especially when it's as frequently drop dead gorgeous as GTA 6.

The slightly lower framerates haven't affected the game's critical response so far, either. In Eurogamer's GTA 6 review, our Chris Tapsell called it a "game of opposites and awe, minute detail and impossible scale" as "Rockstar pushes back the horizon of video games once again."

If you're planning to jump into the game at midnight - or if you're virtually travelling to New Zealand for early entry - there's a few things to be aware of. First is that you won't be able to replay GTA 6's missions without multiple save files, so be sure to soak it all up. Second, some Ultimate Edition content is only available in the first chapter.

Grand Theft Auto 6 leaker Cyberleek appears to have followed through on their threat to release the executable of the Xbox build of GTA 6 they put into the wild last week, calling it "an early Christmas gift" for followers and explicitly linking the leak to efforts to recreate the game on PC: "The torch passes to the open source recomp and emulation projects."

Cyberleek released a near-complete build of GTA 6 late last week, holding back only the main exe—the part that makes everything else run, basically—until either their crypto coin achieved a $15 million market cap, or November 23, whichever came first. The crypto missed badly, but time marches on, and so here we are.

The release of the exe, naturally, includes a call for more "donations" in its readme file (via Reddit) which Cyberleek said will go toward a secretive project "for the gamers." They also taunted Take-Two Interactive's efforts to track them down: "Months of takedowns, subpoenas and wallet tracing later, the hunt is still on and the uploads keep arriving. No budget makes a lock unbreakable, and no court order deletes what the internet already has."

Leaks in the game industry aren't anything new, but this case is unique: GTA 6, effectively the biggest videogame of all time, still hasn't been announced for PC, as is Take-Two's way. But the advent of AI means the game could be emulated on our platform far more quickly than was possible in the past—some modders estimated it could happen within a week.

One of the leads on the Leonida recomp project predicted that things will start to move quickly from here:

At the same time, Shayder tempered expectations in a message on the Leonida Discord, saying "it will take at least a week" for the project to reach the point where GTA will be playable on PC.

How that unofficial emulated made-with-AI build would compare to the real deal is an open question, and I strongly suspect the answer will be "not well," but even just having something GTA 6-ish playable on PC is a headache that I'm pretty sure Take-Two would rather not have to deal with. I also wonder whether it will prompt Take-Two to release GTA 6 on PC more quickly than it has with previous releases. A rumor to that effect surfaced in October and I had serious doubts, but it's possible that ongoing emulation efforts will expedite its arrival..

#3806. Valve are pausing Steam Machine 2TB orders over "supply constraints," though the 512GB model is free of its waitlist

Valve giveth, and Valve taketh away in their latest Steam Machine availability update. The dinky SteamOS PC continues to have a terrible time with AI industry-inflicted hardware parts shortages, which at least for its flagship 2TB model, have become such a problem that Valve are suspending new orders until further notice. While Valve's post says that they "have wrapped up sending purchase invites out to all remaining 2TB reservation holders" – meaning if you'd previously reserved one, you'll still get your chance to buy – "supply restraints" have put the kibosh on any new orders for now.

It's not all bad news, though. The cheaper 512GB Steam Machine has achieved "add-to-cart status", which is Valve's slightly odd way of saying you can snap one up without having to join a reservation waitlist. Just like in the Before Times! The post does add that 512GB stock is still limited, so that might sell out too if they can't source enough parts to build new ones, though this is still the first time that the refreshed Steam Machine has been waitlist-free since launching in June.

One could, with the aid of a Torx screwdriver and a conveniently illustrated guide, work around the 2TB model's lack of existence by nabbing a readily available 512GB Machine and replacing its stock SSD with a chunkier aftermarket drive. A not-terrible, budget two-gigster can be had from £240, which when added to the 512GB Machine's £879 outlay, actually works out a little less than buying a 2TB Machine as is. SteamOS is free to download and install, and swapping out the Steam Machine's SSD is considerably easier than the plasticky brain surgery of Steam Deck drive replacement.

Of course, ideally none of that would be necessary, and we could all fill our living rooms with sub-£700 Steam Machines that had never been choked by the greedy hands of industrial-scale RAM hoarders. But that's not the world we live in. Indeed, Valve end the post by rather chillingly suggesting that their hardware prices may rise yet again.

"We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units," they say, "but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels; as a result we don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we'll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained."

"We anticipate having more information to share come January."

#3805. GTA 6 won't let you use cheats until you complete the main story, and locks progression when you do

Here's a twist: you can't use cheats in Grand Theft Auto 6 until you complete the entire game's main story.

That's what we discovered from our tests at least, after loading in saves at various points through the game to be sure, and it's also both a first for the series and a departure even from how developer Rockstar handled cheats in Red Dead Redemption 2. In that game,approximately half of the cheats were available from the off, and the other half required discovering specific newspapers from around the game's world to unlock.

In GTA 6, you'll again need to do some legwork. This time it appears that all of the game's cheats not only require you to finish the story, but also complete various tasks or challenges to unlock them.

The way it works is simple enough. Once you finish the main story, the "Cheats" tab - previously hidden - quietly appears at the far end of the Progress menu, accessible when you open the in-game map and scroll with the bumper buttons. From there, you can view various sub-sections of cheats, sorted by category, and a list of 10 or so cheats for each.

With each cheat there'll be a short explanation of what it does, and what's required to unlock it and, once unlocked, guidance on how to perform it. This is done via whipping out your phone, holding down the shoulder buttons and using various D-Pad inputs - much the same as GTA 5.

There's also another caveat to bear in mind: when you use a cheat, you'll see a notification warning you that the game can't be saved while it's active, and that Trophies and Achievements are also disabled until you end that session. This makes sense, once you understand the nature of GTA 6's story - there is a cheat for giving yourself a load of money, for instance; another departure from GTA 5 where that popular cheat was removed - but given you'll need certain amounts of cash at various points of the story, enabling you to shortcut that would disrupt the way the narrative unfolds.

We'll have a guide from yours truly to all the game's cheats live on Eurogamer in the very near future, as the game releases here in the UK. In the meantime, if you find yourself on the fence about this one, be sure to give our GTA 6 review a look. As I put it there, giving the game five stars: it is "the most believable and unbelievable video game world ever made".

A new Slay the Spire 2 beta branch update is here, and to no one's surprise, the roguelike's newest and most overpowered character, The Fool, has been hit with plenty of nerfs.

The Fool was added to the beta branch earlier this month, and it was immediately clear that they wouldn't be allowed to exist in their initial state forever. Even at the time, developer Mega Crit said that "we expect to make a great number of content and balance changes before the Fool is ready for the main branch," and lo and behold, the first batch of those is already here.

Mega Crit describes patch v0.114.0 as "mostly Fool-centric," and for good reason – the section covering their changes makes up the vast majority of the patch notes. Not all the changes are nerfs, mind you – a new card has been added called Optimism, which lets you "exhaust ALL Sadness in your Hand. Draw 1 card for each card Exhausted."

Some cards have also been reworked – Arrow Stab, for example, now deals more damage and will see you "gain 6(8) Aim," but no longer has the previous extra effect: "If you have an Arrow, put a card that can Shoot from your Discard Pile into your Hand."

But, yes, there are rather a lot of nerfs, too. In fact, by my count, 20 of The Fool's cards have been nerfed – though I should point out that Cho Ready has been listed twice with slightly different changes, so it's not entirely clear what's going on there. Otherwise, though, nerfs include damage being decreased for Violent Chord, Wah Hammer, Repeat Shot, and The Tower, and block gain being reduced for Lullaby, Song Path, Cho Firm, Wah Cho Ki, and Cho Ready – though again, it's not clear by quite how much for the latter due to that apparent typo.

As you might expect, responses have been… mixed. Some are on board, with one comment on Reddit reading: "A lot of valid changes to Fool. A lot of those cards were really strong, and the nerfs make sense. Make some cards a lot less of an instant grab in every situation, buffed a few of the underperformers. Sad to see some of them, like Cho Ready is taking a big hit, but it was already so strong it's probably for the best."

Meanwhile, one player on Twitter reckons Mega Crit "might've gone a little overboard here," saying: "Fool was a glass cannon, and now she's just an inconsistent hodgepodge. Most of these changes just acknowledge overall power while sacrificing design and synergy. Why nerf the Tarots too? They're inconsistent as is."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Being in the beta branch, of course, there's still every chance that The Fool will face even more significant tweaks yet – and it's not like they can't be nerfed or buffed further when they arrive in the main branch. Either way, though, major changes were to be expected.

Slay the Spire 2 devs declare the "perfect card," and of course it's one I thought was bad.

#3803. GTA 6 leaker claims to have lobbed a near-complete Xbox build of Rockstar's crimsim onto the net, shouts that the "community will have it emulated inside a week"

Cyberleek, the GTA 6 leaker or leakers who shared a bunch of alleged gameplay earlier this year, are now claiming to have released a nearly complete in-development build of the crimsim's Xbox version. Continuing their established grift, the leaker or leakers are threatening to release the main executable file they've withheld unless people pump up the value of their cryptocurrency.

"It is done," a statement posted on Cyberleek’s website claimed. "CL holds the full November 2026 build of Grand Theft Auto VI, and it is going out by torrent. Now. Every file except one - the main executable - held on a countdown. Honest terms, as always: it is an Xbox build this time, not a PC build. CL does not care. This community will have it emulated inside a week, running far past 30fps. CL told you not to preorder for a reason. This is one of the reasons."

So, more anime villain chatter from Cyberleek, who claim the executable file is on a timer and will be released immediately if their crypto coin reaches a $15 million market cap. It looks like the build is yet to be confirmed as genuine.

If any build leak were to result in GTA 6 being emulated on PC in rapid fashion, that would threaten to undercut an official port. Rockstar have yet to confirm that such a port is on the way and when it'll drop, but an October report from GamesBeat claimed the first three months of 2027 as the window in which Rockstar plan to deliver the game to PC. Former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij recently told our Edwin he reckons that concerns about unofficial ports based on the console version of GTA 6, likely made with generative AI, might lead Rockstar not to leave too big a gap before bringing the crimsim to PC officially.

Any alleged playable unofficial port of GTA 6 made with help from genAI and chucked online could, of course, just be a great big pile of malware.

Rockstar, who previously called the initial barrage of leaks laid claim to by Cyberleek "heartbreaking", as well as parent company Take-Two, looked to have begun a hunt for the identity of the leakers back in August.

#3802. Delete GTA 6 from your hard drive and indie publisher Devolver Digital might give you a free game

GTA 6 is out at midnight everywhere (19th November), but it's far from the only game in town. Indie publisher Devolver Digital is taking on the open-world behemoth with its very own Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed, out the same day, and you can win a free copy of the platformer by proving you've deleted GTA 6 off your hard drive.

"Want a free copy of November's hottest release? Repost this tweet with a video of you deleting your GTA6 pre-load along with #MakeRoomForVolvy for a chance to win a copy of Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed on Steam," the publisher wrote on social media.

It's not every day you see a publisher promote its own games by asking folks to delete another company's release, but arguably the wildest part of the giveaway is that Volvy's Adventure isn't launching on consoles. Even if you were to scrub GTA 6's 212GB pre-load from your PS5 or Xbox, you're definitely not making room for Volvy.

"Heads up: Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed is launching exclusively on PC. While we expect to see console GTA deletions in your submissions, Steam keys are the only prize available for this giveaway," Devolver noted.

Devolver made quite an amusing GTA 6 parody trailer, as well, which sees Volvy and Miss Volvy running from the police and getting steamy in the shower. I've embedded it up above for your viewing pleasure.

For the unaware, Volvy used to be a common fixture at Devolver Digital's frequently bonkers notE3 presentations. He's now somewhat of a company mascot. But while Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed is being presented as a "much-anticipated remaster of the original remake of the hit action-platformer," this is, in fact, Volvy's first proper game. Making up an elaborate history for Volvy is just part of the publisher's long-running and increasingly questionable gag.

Gunbrella and Gato Robot developer doinksoft is behind this one, a throwback side-scrolling platformer where our mouse-like mascot uses his oversized hand to helicopter over gaps, punch through roadblocks and, erm, fist himself underground, per the game's Steam page.

Devolver Digital has been waiting to steal Rockstar's thunder for well over a year now. The publisher threatened to release a game on GTA 6's release date way back in May 2025, and has pushed back its plan with each new GTA 6 delay. Gotta respect the commitment, at least.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"I think the version of BioWare that survives EA better is a version where we drop down to one franchise at a time, maybe just one franchise at all. Maybe we just carve SWTOR off and they become an independent studio within EA, because I don't know how what I'm about to say makes sense if you don't do that. But you ship Mass Effect, you ship Dragon Age, and then one of those wins—I hate this—one of those wins and then you just become a one-project studio. There are lots of studios within EA that did that and it didn't work—they still got murdered in their sleep, so maybe that doesn't work anyway." Via an interview with Pembridge.

Many are asking themselves how a legendary studio like BioWare, which is responsible for staples of the PC gaming genre like Neverwinter Nights, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, and the OG Baldur's Gate, alongside Mass Effect and Dragon Age, can be shuttered.

Former Dragon Age executive producer Mark Darrah has already explained how the studio was backed into a corner by EA. Escalating financial pressure led to the poor decisions and subpar games we saw ahead of BioWare's closure. But what if it had all gone differently? Despite everything, Darrah does question whether there was a way for BioWare to survive under EA.

"BioWare's entire existence under EA—it was essentially zero sum, if somebody was getting resources it was coming at the expense of somebody else," Darrah explains. "It's almost like BioWare has run exactly the same way for its entire existence. But the external constraints were different. So in the early days when BioWare needed more people it hired more people. That's like Baldur's Gate 1, Neverwinter Nights, in the early days when we have all these different threads and branches.

"And then in 2007/2008, when the EA constraints come in, the same desires are there, we need more people to ship our games so the way we fix that in that time period is by cutting off all those other branches. So [Jade Empire sequel] Revolver goes away and the Handheld [Development] Group goes away … and so Dragon Age and Mass Effect eats everything."

The alternative? Scaling things down to meet EA's needs. "Budgets keep going up, but we're still not getting bigger… So what's happening is that the walls are closing in and we're trying to be three things [SWTOR, Mass Effect, Dragon Age] and arguably we can only afford to be two things, or one thing." There's no telling whether this would've saved BioWare, but it has worked for other studios.

"Maxis figured out how to live inside of EA and BioWare never did," Darrah adds. Focusing on just one project does seem to be the answer, or at least Darrah believes it has been for Maxis and Battlefield Studios, which both had games that initially underperformed and weren't well received. "If [Battlefield Studios] don't work on Battlefield then you might as well shut the studio down. So they all work on Battlefield 4 and they fix Battlefield 4 and it becomes successful, like very successful after the fact. The Sims 4, same thing."

On the other hand "Mass Effect Andromeda ships and then Dragon Age 4 which has been starving for resources is like 'No, no [the devs] are supposed to come to us. Where are they?' That need to keep them in place isn't there in the same way. So when I say BioWare didn't adapt to EA, that's what I mean."

#3799. Amid a year of layoffs, Ubisoft yank the cover off Motherbrain, their new studio "focused on AI for gameplay innovation"

Something something "proprietary technologies for gameplay to empower creators" something something

Ubisoft have revealed their Motherbrain. It's far less cool than it sounds. Rather than being a giant floating slab of thinky meat that can do telepathy, Motherbrain is a studio dedicated to doing development stuff with generative AI. As you might expect, it consists of the folks who worked on Ubisoft's "first playable generative AI experience".

Motherbrain's reveal as "a dedicated subsidiary focused on AI for gameplay innovation" came via Ubisoft's latest earnings report, where the company trumpeted that their "new operating model" is "now fully in place". The model is the reorganising into creative houses responsible for different game series that Ubisoft announced at the start of this year, with leaders for all of the houses now arranged.

"We have also established Motherbrain, the team behind our first playable generative AI experience Teammates, as a dedicated subsidiary developing proprietary technologies for gameplay to empower creators and open up new possibilities for richer, more immersive and engaging player experiences," CEO Yves Guillemot said.

You'll never guess what his next few lines were. "We remain on track with our cost reduction program, reflecting our commitment to a focused and disciplined organization as we are preparing for a significantly stronger content cycle," the exec said. "In parallel, we have made progress on our refinancing plan with the objective of securing competitive terms and putting in place an efficient medium-term plan over the coming months."

That'd be the wave of layoffs and closures Ubisoft have been rolling out all through this year, most recently getting rid of 166 staff at Ubisoft Montreal and Ubisoft Quebec, both of which worked on Assassin's Creed Shadows. Ubisoft Singapore and Trials developers Redlynx, Ubisoft Winnipeg, Belgrade, and Barcelona, long-time Tom Clancy studio Red Storm, Ubisoft's Paris HQ and three German studios including Anno devs Ubisoft Mainz are all on the list of bits of the company affected in some way by the cuts.

Changes to remote working policies have also contributed to strikes at Ubisoft studios in France and Italy.

Ah well, at least there's seemingly money there to support the developing of those proprietary technologies infused with genAI brainiacery.

#3798. GTA 6's Japanese version only partially obscures male nudity by putting Jason in a thong, seemingly due to regional censorship

GTA 6 is slowly rolling out across the globe. The crime epic's already available to play in countries such as South Korea and New Zealand, but Japanese players are finding out that male nudity is only partially obscured by a thin black thong that covers Jason and the other men in Leonida.

Last week, we reported that GTA 6 might have been censored in Japan since the region's age rating board lacked any mention of the "sexual content" we knew it would include elsewhere. The Japanese version's install size was also notably smaller than other places in the world.

Now that GTA 6 is finally in the hands of players, we have a better idea of what was left out and/or covered up in Japan. Multiple social media accounts playing the game in Japan have reported that when you take main man Jason into the shower, his butt is only kinda covered up by a thong. GTA 6 censorship on the Japanese version is kinda funny lol https://t.co/u8v0f0cqz0

Another social media post spots a different male NPC wearing a very similar black thong during a cutscene that normally has him laid bare in international versions of the game. I'm guessing all instances of male nudity might be obscured similarly in GTA 6's Japanese version.

GTA 6 is far from the only game that's dealt with regional censorship in Japan, however. Baldur's Gate 3 and The Witcher 3 had their most salacious scenes censored in some manner, for example. And even GTA 5 had to remove its infamous torture scene for approval in Japan. It's quite possible GTA 6 has had to cover more than just the backside of nude men to go on sale in the country, although those regional differences won't become entirely clear until players get further through the story.

Ahead of the game's full launch, GTA 6 managed to break Reddit and viewership records on platforms like YouTube and Twitch. Interesting tidbits are also flying out on release day, like the fact you can't replay missions or use cheats until finishing the story. "A game of opposites and awe, minute detail and impossible scale, Rockstar pushes back the horizon of video games once again with GTA 6. Finding the Ocelot Jugular in GTA 6, like a bunch of other cars Randy wants from you, is no easy feat. Unlike your previous car heisting quests, you aren't given the location of the motors Randy's client is after, so you just have to keep your eye open when you're out and about, specifically in more affluent areas.

All the cars on Randy's list, including the Ocelot Jugular, can be found in multiple GTA 6 locations, making this a little easier, so keep your eyes peeled outside Vice City nightclubs and casinos, for example. If you want things to be a little easier, though, I've got the location of a guaranteed spawn below.

The Ocelot Jugular can be found around Vice City, particularly at lively hotspots after dark, but there's a guaranteed spawn in Belville, parked in a garage in a cul-de-sac as marked on the map above.

Grabbing the Ocelot from this location at least means you can get another of Randy's cars checked off fast, without having to hunt around for days. Even better, it respawns the every morning, meaning you can go and take one for yourself, too, provided you've got the cash to pay for registration.

While we're on the topic of GTA 6 cars, make sure you also go take a look at Paul Walker's GTA 6 car, inspired by his (or Brian O'Conner's) Mitsubishi Eclipse in the original 1995 Fast and Furious movie. That one's far cheaper to register than the Ocelot, and I'd argue it's cooler and drives better, to boot.

#3795. It really seems like Xbox isn't allowed to say GTA 6 at all

Like many major brands, Xbox is finding all sorts of ways to associate with the biggest game launch of the year: Grand Theft Auto 6. Unlike indie publisher Devolver Digital, however, Xbox has cleverly avoided ever mentioning GTA 6 directly in its marketing campaigns for GTA 6.

As pointed out by multiple people on social media, the Xbox Wire post titled 'How to Get Ready for November 19' is one all about celebrating the big release day of GTA 6, and helping players find ways to maximise their time with their Xbox consoles. Despite that, it does not mention GTA 6 by name a single time.

"Birthdays, anniversaries, and holidays have come and gone, but this day belongs to you and your Xbox console," the post reads, stopping short of saying why the day is important. "We can hardly believe it's almost here, either."

One day prior, Xbox Wire partnered with DJ Khaled to create custom doctor's notes for players to submit to their employers to take the day off. Why would you want to take 19th November off? Because you're apparently having "a serious case of Vitamin G deficiency".

Going even further back, Xbox revealed a custom-made Series X console it called X-Bite, which is a large, sculpted alligator that swallowed a Series X console. Why? Because "this November, Xbox is heading to Florida - home to incredible wildlife, unforgettable places, and every now and then, stories you have to see to believe."

Florida, of course, is the real-world US state GTA 6's Leonida is based on, but in keeping with the theme of not referring to the game - or its made-up state - directly, the blog does not.

Now, Xbox has directly named GTA 6 in places, but only when, seemingly, the post is about factual information. This Xbox Wire post reiterates GTA 6's Xbox Cloud streaming availability, and this one is a look-ahead at games launching the following week on Xbox. But that's about the extent of what you can expect.

So what's going on here? The simple guess is that PlayStation has a co-marketing deal with Rockstar, meaning no other console platform gets to use GTA 6's name in marketing. Sony is allowed to make custom, GTA 6-themed consoles, branded, limited-edition DualSense controllers and blaster the game all over the PS Blog, social media, and even change the PS App's icon colour to match the hue of GTA 6's.

This is all too similar to when, each year, various brands encourage you to buy their products to be ready for The Big Game, which is very distinct from the Super Bowl happening on the same day. Like Xbox, those brands simply don't have the rights to the real thing.

GTA 6 is available now on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. In Eurogamer's five-star review, Chris Tapsell wrote, "Rockstar pushes back the horizon of video games once again with GTA 6. An irreducible mix of silliness, intimacy, grand ideas and rock 'n' roll action - and a load more after that."
